desc:
A row of tiles is described by a string s of lowercase letters. Whenever two neighbouring tiles carry the same letter x, they merge into one tile with the next letter of the alphabet (a, a become b; b, b become c; and so on). Two neighbouring 'z' tiles cannot grow any further and simply disappear. A merged tile can immediately merge again with a neighbour.

Repeat while two equal neighbours exist, always merging the leftmost such pair first, and return the final string. It may be empty.

Examples: 'aaa' becomes 'ba'. 'aab' becomes 'bb' and then 'c'. 'zzab' becomes 'ab'.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
The answer may be the empty string
hints: After a merge the new tile may be equal to its left neighbour, so merges can cascade backwards through the already processed part.
Because the leftmost pair is always handled first, everything left of the current position never contains an equal pair. Process tiles one at a time.

Keep a stack of settled tiles. For each incoming letter, while the top of the stack equals it, pop the top and replace the incoming letter by the next one (dropping it completely after a pair of 'z'); then push what is left.
editorial: Scan from left to right with a stack of tiles that currently have no equal neighbours. When a new letter c comes, compare it with the top. If they are equal, both tiles merge: pop the top and let the new letter become c + 1 (or vanish if c was 'z'). The merged tile is now the incoming tile and may again equal the new top, so repeat. When the loop ends, push the tile if it still exists.

This is exactly the leftmost-pair-first process: the stack holds the prefix, in which no pair exists, so the leftmost pair is always the one formed by the incoming tile and the top. Each merge reduces the number of tiles by one, and each letter is pushed at most once, so the total work is O(n) amortised. The final stack is the answer.
